<reason>Both sides were excellent, grounded, and used the Q/A format cleanly. A's rhetoric was the best in the debate and its grievance-formation attack on "the grievance is the trigger" landed hard. But B built the more durable architecture: the standard-vs-machinery distinction survived A's "the score IS the standard" merger, and B's standing-vs-triggered frame became the debate's actual decision rule. Decisively, B caught A in an internal tension A never repaired: under A's own clarified "materiality" design, the worker still never sees the threshold, so the motion does not fix A's own opening vignette. B also won the regulator half with the unanswered dynamism dilemma (stale snapshot vs. version-by-version treadmill) and mapped A's mid-debate clarifications (asymmetric disclosure, function-split for theft models, size thresholds) as a convergence toward existing notice law. A's execution also cost it: two clipped turns, including its R2 weighing, and a closing that left B4.1 and B4.5 standing while pivoting to pattern-detection, which B answered with triggered investigation. B simply left fewer live burdens unanswered.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 [B4.1]: under PRO's own asymmetric design workers get "materiality," never the threshold — so A's jammed-scanner worker is fired at an unseen number in A's world too, and only adversarial contest actually exposes the bad count. A never answered it, and B4.4's concession-mapping compounded the damage.</best_rebuttal>
